culture:Sagrada Família — the tallest ch.name: Sagrada Família
culture:Sagrada Família — the tallest ch.teaser: Begun in 1882, blessed under its 172.5 m central spire in June 2026, and still not finished
culture:Sagrada Família — the tallest ch.story: Work began in 1882 and Antoni Gaudí gave the last 43 years of his life to it; he was knocked down by a tram on Carrer de Bailèn in June 1926 and died days later. A century on, on 10 June 2026, Pope Leo XIV said mass inside and blessed the newly topped Tower of Jesus Christ, 172.5 metres, which makes this the tallest church in the world. Inside, the columns branch like trees and the stained glass throws green and blue on the east side in the morning, red and orange on the west late in the day. Cranes remain: the main façade is unfinished.
culture:Sagrada Família — the tallest ch.why: Go early on a weekday for the cool colours through the east windows, and book the tower option if you want height.
facts: Daily; hours change with the season, so check the official site
€26 entry, €36 with a tower; guided options more (Oct 2026, check sagradafamilia.org)

culture:Casa Batlló & La Pedrera — the P.name: Casa Batlló & La Pedrera
culture:Casa Batlló & La Pedrera — the P.teaser: Two Gaudí houses on one avenue: a dragon's back at no. 43, a stone cliff at no. 92
culture:Casa Batlló & La Pedrera — the P.story: Gaudí remodelled Casa Batlló, at Passeig de Gràcia 43, for a textile family: balconies shaped like bone and jaw, a roof ridge scaled like a dragon's back, and a light well tiled from deep to pale blue so the daylight evens out down the floors. Walk about seven minutes up the avenue to Casa Milà at no. 92, which Barcelona nicknamed La Pedrera, the quarry, for its waving stone front with no straight lines. Its roof terrace is a field of helmeted chimneys and ventilation towers you walk among. Seeing both in one afternoon shows the same architect doing opposite things.
culture:Casa Batlló & La Pedrera — the P.why: If you only have time for one roof, take La Pedrera's chimneys; if one interior, Casa Batlló's blue light well.
facts: Passeig de Gràcia 43 (Batlló) and 92 (La Pedrera), Eixample
Daily; check each site for the day's hours and night sessions

art:Casa Vicens.name: Casa Vicens
art:Casa Vicens.teaser: The first house Gaudí built, 1883–85: green, cream and marigold tiles, and a young architect finding his way
art:Casa Vicens.story: Before the Sagrada Família, before Passeig de Gràcia, there was this summer house for the stockbroker Manuel Vicens, built 1883 to 1885 when Gaudí was barely thirty. The street front is a checkerboard of green and cream tile with a marigold motif, and inside are painted ceilings, a smoking room with a Moorish honeycomb vault, and fake-perspective birds on the walls. It became a house museum only in 2017, so it is the least crowded of his major works. Here you watch a vocabulary being tried out that later grew into the others.
art:Casa Vicens.why: Come for the smoking room ceiling, and for the quiet you will not get at his bigger houses.
facts: Carrer de les Carolines 20, Gràcia (Metro L3 Fontana)

culture:MUHBA Plaça del Rei — Roman Barc.name: MUHBA Plaça del Rei
culture:MUHBA Plaça del Rei — Roman Barc.teaser: Take the lift down from a medieval square and walk the streets of Roman Barcino
culture:MUHBA Plaça del Rei — Roman Barc.story: Barcelona began as a small Roman colony, founded around 15 to 10 BC under Augustus with the long name Iulia Augusta Faventia Paterna Barcino. Under the Plaça del Rei, walkways carry you over its excavated floor: a fullery where cloth was washed and dyed, vats and presses for wine, salting tanks, and later an early Christian basilica and bishop's palace. Climb back up and you come out in the Gothic halls of the Palau Reial Major, the medieval royal palace, including the great arched Saló del Tinell. Two thousand years of the city stacked in one block.
culture:MUHBA Plaça del Rei — Roman Barc.why: The best single hour for understanding how old the city under your feet really is.
facts: Tue–Sat 10:00–19:00, Sun 10:00–20:00, closed Mon (Oct 2026, MUHBA site)

culture:Palau de la Música Catalana.name: Palau de la Música Catalana
culture:Palau de la Música Catalana.teaser: A 1908 concert hall built for a choir, lit through a ceiling of stained glass
culture:Palau de la Música Catalana.story: Lluís Domènech i Montaner built the Palau for the Orfeó Català, a choral society, and it opened in 1908. Every surface is working: mosaic muses half sunk into the stage wall, a carved stone burst of Catalan folk song on the street corner, columns faced in tiled flowers, and overhead an inverted dome of stained glass, gold at its centre and blue around the rim, that lets daylight into a concert hall. UNESCO listed it in 1997 with his Hospital de Sant Pau. It is still a working hall with a full season, so a concert is the truest way to see it.
culture:Palau de la Música Catalana.why: Book a daytime concert or visit to see the glass with sun behind it; at night it is lit from inside.

culture:Museu Picasso.name: Museu Picasso
culture:Museu Picasso.teaser: Five medieval palaces on Carrer Montcada holding the painter's early years and his Meninas
culture:Museu Picasso.story: Picasso arrived in Barcelona at 13 in 1895 and stayed, on and off, until 1904; his Blue Period began here after the suicide of his friend Carles Casagemas. The museum opened in 1963 on the initiative of his secretary Jaume Sabartés, and in 1970 Picasso himself gave a large gift of his early work. It fills five Gothic palaces joined together along Carrer Montcada, courtyards and stone staircases included. Most visitors rush for the famous names; the surprise is the boy's academic drawings, and at the end the 58-canvas series of 1957 in which he took apart Velázquez's Las Meninas.
culture:Museu Picasso.why: Spend the time on the teenage drawings and the Meninas room; together they show the whole arc.
facts: Tue–Sun; check the official site for hours
€15 (seen Jul 2026; guides quote €12–15 in 2026). Free Thursday 16:00–19:00 in winter and the first Sunday of the month, booked online in advance

art:Fundacio Joan Miro.name: Fundació Joan Miró
art:Fundacio Joan Miro.teaser: Miró's own foundation, in Josep Lluís Sert's white building of courtyards and top light
art:Fundacio Joan Miro.story: Miró wanted a working centre, not a shrine, and his friend Josep Lluís Sert designed it: white walls, vaulted roof lights that pull daylight down onto the paintings, patios and roof terraces laid out in a spiral so you circle the collection and come back out to the trees. It opened in 1975 and turned fifty in 2025. Inside is one of the most complete collections of his work anywhere, from early paintings to the large, nearly empty late canvases and the big woven tapestry, with a room kept for young contemporary artists.
art:Fundacio Joan Miro.why: Walk the roof terraces between rooms: the sculptures stand against the sky the way Sert planned.
facts: Tue–Sun, closed most Mondays; check the official site
€17 online, €18 at the door (Oct 2026, from guides; check the official site)

art:MNAC (Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalu.name: MNAC
art:MNAC (Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalu.teaser: Whole church apses lifted from the Pyrenees, rebuilt inside a 1929 palace above Plaça d'Espanya
art:MNAC (Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalu.story: In the early twentieth century, as dealers began stripping Pyrenean churches, Catalan curators had their painted walls peeled off and brought to Barcelona. The result is the best Romanesque mural collection in the world: whole apses rebuilt at their original curve, with Christ in Majesty from Sant Climent de Taüll staring down in reds and ochres. The building is the Palau Nacional, put up for the 1929 International Exhibition. Upstairs the collection runs through Gothic altarpieces to Modernista furniture and painting, and the roof terraces look straight down the axis to the sea.
art:MNAC (Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalu.why: Go first to the Romanesque rooms, then up to the terraces for the view over the city.
facts: €12 general; €2 basic ticket for the building and terraces only. Free Saturdays from 15:00 and the first Sunday of the month, booked online (Oct 2026, check)

art:MACBA (Museu d'Art Contemporani de B.name: MACBA
art:MACBA (Museu d'Art Contemporani de B.teaser: Richard Meier's white museum in the Raval, with the city's skaters clattering on the plaza outside
art:MACBA (Museu d'Art Contemporani de B.story: Richard Meier's building opened in November 1995: a long white box of glass, ramps and skylights set down among the old Raval tenements on Plaça dels Àngels. The plaza in front became one of the best known skate spots in Europe, so the soundtrack to any visit is wheels on stone and the crack of boards. Inside, there is no fixed canon on the walls; the collection of post-1945 Catalan, Spanish and international art goes up in changing hangs, alongside research-heavy and often politically sharp exhibitions.
art:MACBA (Museu d'Art Contemporani de B.why: Sit on the plaza steps before or after; the skaters are as much a part of the place as the art.

art:CCCB (Centre de Cultura Contemporani.name: CCCB
art:CCCB (Centre de Cultura Contemporani.teaser: No permanent collection, by design: big essay exhibitions in an old almshouse in the Raval
art:CCCB (Centre de Cultura Contemporani.story: The CCCB opened in 1994 inside the Casa de Caritat, the city's eighteenth and nineteenth century poorhouse. Architects Helio Piñón and Albert Viaplana left the old patio and grafted on a sheer modern wing whose top floor leans out in a dark glass sheet that reflects the rooftops and the sea behind them. There is no collection to see; instead it builds large exhibitions that argue a case, about cities, technology, the climate or a single writer, and runs talks, film and festivals around them. Check what is on before you go.
art:CCCB (Centre de Cultura Contemporani.why: Stand in the courtyard and look up at the leaning glass wall reflecting the skyline.

art:Disseny Hub Barcelona (DHUB).name: Disseny Hub Barcelona
art:Disseny Hub Barcelona (DHUB).teaser: The city's design museum, in the cantilevered block locals call the stapler
art:Disseny Hub Barcelona (DHUB).story: Four old collections — decorative arts, ceramics, textiles and fashion, graphic arts — came together in 2014 in this building by MBM Arquitectes at Plaça de les Glòries. Its top storey juts some 14.5 metres out over a sunken plaza, and Barcelona promptly named it la grapadora, the stapler. The museum treats objects as social history: a chair, a dress or a tile as evidence of how people lived. Expect thematic shows on how things shape daily life, with tens of thousands of objects held behind them.
art:Disseny Hub Barcelona (DHUB).why: Pair it with the Glòries area around it, where the city has rebuilt a motorway junction as a park.
facts: Plaça de les Glòries Catalanes 37–38 (Metro L1 Glòries)

craft:Do this one.name: Mosaiccos
craft:Do this one.teaser: Break tile and set a trencadís in El Born, taught by a Generalitat-accredited master craftswoman
craft:Do this one.story: Trencadís is the broken-tile mosaic that Gaudí and Josep Maria Jujol used to skin curved walls and benches in Modernista Barcelona. At Mosaiccos, a studio a few doors from the Museu Picasso, you learn it hands on: nippers, shards, a pattern drawn on a board. Projects include the Passeig de Gràcia hexagonal paving tile and the panot that floors the city's streets. The studio is run by Angelika Heinbach, a German-born artist working in Spain for more than 26 years, who holds the Generalitat's mestre artesà accreditation; sources give different years for it. Honest point: this is a revived technique, not an old family workshop.
craft:Do this one.why: The one Barcelona craft class we found with a named, accredited master and open booking; your piece goes home with you.
facts: Cut and set a trencadís mosaic; the studio grouts it, and you collect it later the same day or the next

craft:Other one.name: La Manual Alpargatera
craft:Other one.teaser: Espadrilles sewn on Carrer d'Avinyó since just after the Civil War, at a bench in use since 1940
craft:Other one.story: The shop opened in the 1940s, just after the Civil War, and has never moved. At the back, a small workshop still works at a table in use since 1940, hand-stitching jute soles to canvas, and the sales staff are trained to make espadrilles themselves. Demand outgrew the back room: a larger workshop in Horta now helps make the 30,000 to 40,000 pairs of the basic model sold each year. Who founded it is told two ways: one account names Juan Olivé and Emilia Martínez, another Joana Martínez and Francisco Tàsies. Missing: a class. You can watch and buy, but you cannot enrol.
craft:Other one.why: Buy the plain jute-and-canvas pair, made in the city, and look through to the bench at the back.

craft:Other two.name: Cereria Subirà
craft:Other two.teaser: Barcelona's oldest shop still trading, selling candles since 1761
craft:Other two.story: The candle shop was founded in 1761 on Carrer dels Corders and moved in 1847 to Baixada de la Presó 7, the street now called Baixada de la Llibreteria, where it still stands a minute from the cathedral. It is listed by the city as an Establiment Emblemàtic and is widely called the oldest shop in Barcelona still trading. The Subirà family has run it since 1939. Inside: votive candles, tall church tapers, scented and coloured ones in rows. Missing: a class. It is a shop, not a workshop you can join.
craft:Other two.why: Step in for the room and a church taper; it is the oldest counter in the city.
facts: Buy candles; there is no workshop for visitors

craft:What is sold as Barcelona craft.name: What is sold as Barcelona craft
craft:What is sold as Barcelona craft.teaser: Flamenco dolls, Gaudí lizards and 'Barcelona' espadrilles: most Rambla stock tells you nothing of its maker
craft:What is sold as Barcelona craft.story: Walk La Rambla or the Gothic lanes and the same shelves repeat: flamenco dancer dolls and frilled dresses, castanets and fans, resin trencadís lizards, espadrilles stacked by the hundred. Flamenco is an Andalusian art, not the Catalan one; the city's own Roma music is rumba catalana. A trencadís lizard cast in one piece is a picture of Gaudí's broken-tile method, not the method. We found no sourced study of where this stock is made, so we will not quote a figure; the honest test is simpler. A real maker puts a name and an address on the thing, and can tell you who made it.
craft:What is sold as Barcelona craft.why: Ask who made it and where; if nobody can answer, it is a souvenir, not craft.
facts: Buy from a maker with a name: espadrilles at La Manual Alpargatera, candles at Cereria Subirà, a mosaic you set yourself at Mosaiccos (all in this section)
Flamenco is not Catalan, but it has Barcelona roots: the dancer Carmen Amaya was born in the Somorrostro beach settlement, and the city had tablaos for generations

coffee-scene:Cafes El Magnifico.name: Cafés El Magnífico
coffee-scene:Cafes El Magnifico.teaser: Roasting single origins on Carrer de l'Argenteria since 1989, from a family in coffee since 1919
coffee-scene:Cafes El Magnifico.story: The family's coffee trade goes back to a colonial-goods store in 1919 and the El Magnífico name to 1962. The turn came after Salvador Sans met the importer Philippe Jobin in 1987 and began buying traceable fine coffees; in 1989 he opened this roasting shop on Argenteria, where you still order at a wooden counter lined with sacks and tins. Sans has judged the international Cup of Excellence since 2002, his daughter Claudia now runs quality, and in 2018 the family bought La Portorriqueña, a roaster from 1906. The cortado tastes chosen, not blended.
coffee-scene:Cafes El Magnifico.why: Buy whole beans of the current single origin to take back aboard.
facts: A seasonal single-origin filter, or a cortado at the counter

coffee-scene:Nomad Coffee (Coffee Bar, e.name: Nomad Coffee
coffee-scene:Nomad Coffee (Coffee Bar, e.teaser: A monochrome coffee bar down a covered passage, from a two-time Spanish barista champion
coffee-scene:Nomad Coffee (Coffee Bar, e.story: Jordi Mestre won the Spanish Barista Championship in 2012 and 2013 after starting on a London coffee cart in 2011. His Nomad Coffee Lab of 2014 is widely called Barcelona's first dedicated specialty coffee shop, and the roastery now supplies cafés far beyond the city. This bar down Passatge Sert is small and monochrome: a counter, a grinder, shelves of beans, and nothing on the menu but coffee. Staff will steer you to the pour-over of the week.
coffee-scene:Nomad Coffee (Coffee Bar, e.why: Let them choose the pour-over; this is a place to taste, not to brunch.

coffee-scene:SlowMov.name: SlowMov
coffee-scene:SlowMov.teaser: A café and small roastery under Catalan vaults in Gràcia, buying from the same farms year after year
coffee-scene:SlowMov.story: François Justet and Carmen Callizo opened SlowMov in May 2015, among the city's first specialty roasters alongside Nomad. It sits in an old Gràcia house with high ceilings, Catalan brick vaults and mosaic floors, the roaster working on site. The idea is in the name: fewer coffees, bought directly from long-term producers, traceable to the farm, and sold in packaging meant to be reused or recycled. It was among the nominations for Spain's best coffee shops in early 2026.
coffee-scene:SlowMov.why: Order the batch brew of the current long-relationship lot and ask which farm it comes from.
facts: A filter or batch brew of a Brazilian, Ethiopian or Mexican lot

coffee-gardens:Federal Cafe (Sant Antoni.story: Federal is airy and Australian-run, spread over several floors up to a plant-filled roof terrace, and a long-standing stop for remote workers. That communal table has no power sockets, so come charged. Weekends are full and staff can cool on laptops at meal times.

coffee-gardens:Skye Coffee Co.teaser: Espresso pulled from a 1972 Citroën van parked inside a white Poblenou warehouse
coffee-gardens:Skye Coffee Co.story: The counter is a restored 1972 Citroën HY van, the owner a British designer who named the café after herself. coffee-gardens:Biblioteca de Catalunya.name: Biblioteca de Catalunya
coffee-gardens:Biblioteca de Catalunya.teaser: The national library in the stone naves of a fifteenth-century hospital
coffee-gardens:Biblioteca de Catalunya.story: Catalonia's national library fills the Gothic wards of the old Hospital de la Santa Creu, long stone naves under great pointed arches, with a courtyard garden of orange trees outside. The General Reading Room has some 180 places with power and wifi, and the silence of a research library. That is also the catch: this is not a public study hall. Readers must be 18 or over, register with ID for a card, and the rules ask you to justify your need for the collections. It suits a crew member with real research to do, not a casual laptop afternoon.

coffee-gardens:Hotel Casa Fuster — Café.name: Café Vienès, Casa Fuster
coffee-gardens:Hotel Casa Fuster — Café.teaser: Coffee under Domènech i Montaner's columns, and jazz on Thursday nights
coffee-gardens:Hotel Casa Fuster — Café.story: Lluís Domènech i Montaner, the architect of the Palau de la Música, built Casa Fuster between 1908 and 1911 at the top of Passeig de Gràcia, the first building in the city faced in white marble. It is now a hotel, and its ground-floor Café Vienès keeps the period room of columns and tall windows. The café was a gathering place for writers and talkers in its first life, and on Thursday nights it turns into a dinner-and-jazz club with classic jazz and swing.

coffee-gardens:Casa Bonay.name: Casa Bonay & Satan's Coffee Corner
coffee-gardens:Casa Bonay.teaser: An 1869 townhouse with its old tiled floors, good coffee at the door and a lounge for the long afternoon
coffee-gardens:Casa Bonay.story: Casa Bonay is an 1869 Eixample townhouse on Gran Via, turned into a hotel in 2016 by its founder Inés Miró-Sans with the Brooklyn designers Studio Tack, who kept the high ceilings and the original hydraulic-tile floors. On the ground floor, Satan's Coffee Corner, the second branch of one of the city's early specialty bars, pours serious coffee from morning to early evening, and the Libertine lounge beside it is made for spreading out with a laptop. It now trades as Hotel Casa Bonay & Spa, with a rooftop wellness area.
